The reproductive biology of the Hooded butterflyfish (Chaetodon larvatus) begins with external fertilisation during paired spawning events, a common strategy among obligate corallivores inhabiting Red Sea and Gulf of Aden reefs. Gravid females release buoyant, transparent eggs roughly 0.75 mm in diameter, a size consistent with pelagic broadcast spawners that rely on high fecundity rather than parental care. Once fertilised, the embryonated eggs are left to drift in the plankton. Under controlled laboratory conditions set to a constant water temperature of 30 °C [T = 30 °C], the pace of embryonic development accelerates markedly: cleavage, gastrulation, and organogenesis proceed to completion in a window of approximately 1.25 days [ab = approximately 1.25 days] before the chorion ruptures and a thin, endotrophic prolarva emerges. At eclosion, this yolk-sac larva possesses an extraordinarily low body mass, weighing just 0.00023 grams [Wwb = 0.00023 grams]. Such a diminutive starting mass is not unusual among teleost larvae that depend entirely on endogenous yolk reserves during the first days of life, a period that precedes the onset of exogenous feeding. The brevity of the incubation interval at 30 °C underscores the profound thermal sensitivity of developmental rate in this species.

Long-term monitoring of tagged individuals on shallow fore-reef habitats has revealed that Chaetodon larvatus undergoes the transition to reproductive maturity at a relatively small body size. The total length at puberty, defined by the first appearance of ripe gonads during histological examination of biopsy samples, averages 6.7 cm [Lp = 6.7 cm]. At this developmental benchmark, the fish have accumulated a wet body mass of approximately 9.3 grams [Wwp = approximately 9.3 grams]. This early maturation may represent an adaptive response to intense predation pressure or to the ephemeral availability of high-quality coral territories, enabling individuals to commence spawning before being displaced by larger, competitively dominant conspecifics. Comparative data from other obligate corallivorous chaetodontids suggest that Chaetodon larvatus invests in gonadal development at a size far below its asymptotic length, a pattern that likely reflects the trade-off between early reproductive output and continued somatic growth in a resource-limited, thermally dynamic reef environment. Field observations further indicate that the onset of gametogenesis coincides with seasonal peaks in water temperature and food abundance, cues that synchronise first spawning across the population.

Upon reaching full somatic growth, Hooded butterflyfish attain a maximum total length of 12 cm [Li = 12 cm] based on repeated measurements from museum voucher specimens and live captures across their geographic range. The asymptotic wet weight, reflecting the culmination of years of incremental tissue accretion, stabilises at approximately 57 grams [Wwi = approximately 57 grams] in both sexes, although subtle sexual dimorphism in body depth has been noted in some populations. This modest ultimate size is consistent with an obligate corallivorous foraging mode, which demands high maneuverability among branching coral colonies rather than large body mass for territorial defence. In comparison with broader reef piscivores of similar length, the weight-specific metabolic demands of Chaetodon larvatus are elevated, a physiological trait that necessitates nearly constant feeding on Acropora and Pocillopora polyps throughout the day. The combination of small asymptotic mass and high routine activity levels implies a daily energy budget tightly constrained by prey availability, a factor that likely limits population densities on degraded reefs where live coral cover has declined.

The thermal regime that governs developmental rate also shapes adult reproductive allocation. At a sustained water temperature of 30 °C [T = 30 °C], which approximates summer sea surface conditions in the southern Red Sea, sexually mature females exhibit a gonadosomatic index (GSI) of 6% [GSI = 6%] based on whole-body dissections of pre-spawning individuals collected during the peak breeding season. This level of investment, though modest when compared with highly fecund pelagophils, is substantial for a pair-forming, site-attached reef fish that produces small demersal eggs. Concurrently, the species exhibits a protracted natural longevity under these same thermal conditions; captive cohorts maintained at 30 °C have surpassed 25 years [am = 25 years] in age, a lifespan that ranks among the longest documented for any butterflyfish at a temperature of 30 °C [T = 30 °C]. The combination of a relatively early puberty reported earlier and a senescent phase stretched over more than two decades suggests a life history tuned to stable coral reef environments, where adult survival is high and reproductive value accumulates slowly over an extended breeding career.

Unlike many chaetodontids that exhibit dietary plasticity, Chaetodon larvatus remains an obligate corallivore throughout its post-settlement life, a specialization that ties its population dynamics intimately to the health of scleractinian coral communities. Adults form monogamous pairs that jointly defend small territories centered on thickets of Acropora and Pocillopora, within which they forage almost exclusively on coral polyps and associated mucus. This narrow trophic niche renders the species acutely vulnerable to coral bleaching events, which have triggered localised declines in abundance across parts of its range in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden. Behavioural observations indicate that Hooded butterflyfish maintain high diurnal feeding rates, spending up to three-quarters of daylight hours engaged in repeated bites on coral colonies. The energetic returns from such obligate corallivory are limited by the low caloric content of polyp tissue, a constraint that helps explain why growth rates taper off well before the asymptotic total length of 12 cm [Li = 12 cm] is reached. In regions where Acropora cover has been severely reduced, individuals show reduced body condition and diminished reproductive output, confirming that the persistence of this species depends on the integrity of its coral habitat.
